newsitem.title: FRANCE: WPP urges ad agency focus on media-buying.
newsitem.headline: WPP urges ad agency focus on media-buying.

text.p: Martin Sorrell, chairman of WPP Group Plc, the world's largest advertising and marketing services group, criticised advertising agencies for losing media-planning and media-buying business.
He said late on Thursday that other companies were succeeding in snatching away business because ad agencies had not tried hard enough to hold on to it.

Media-planners and media-buyers advise the companies that spend money on advertising -- the "advertisers" -- on how and where to spend their advertising budgets in order best to reach target consumers. Media-buyers then book advertising space -- or "buy the media" -- on behalf of advertisers.

Most global ad agencies offer clients media-planning and media-buying services, but advertisers can also use so-called "media independents" like CIA Group Plc and Carat, which specialise in providing that service.
The Carat Group of companies, Europe's leading media-planning and -buying network, are owned by London-based Aegis Group Plc.
Sorrell, speaking at the International Advertising Festival in the French resort town of Cannes, said Carat and CIA were growing at the expense of ad agencies.
"Why is it that Carat and CIA have grown in Europe?" he asked staff members of Ogilvy & Mather, a global ad agency owned by WPP.
"Because the people who ran advertising agencies did not think it (media-planning and media-buying) was important," he said.

WPP, which also owns J. Walter Thompson and about 40 other marketing services companies worldwide, said on June 20 that it had bought a second chunk of shares in CIA, following an earlier share purchase.
That raised WPP's stake in London-based CIA to 7.8 million shares or 12.8 percent of CIA's issued share capital.
Sorrell also blasted ad agencies for losing business to management consultancies like McKinsey and Co, and Arthur Andersen, and advisers from financial institutions like Goldman Sachs & Co.
He said consultancies were grabbing business away from ad agencies partly because they were more aggressive in marketing their expertise in corporate strategy, including branding strategy.
Sorrell said ad agencies were making a critical mistake in failing to recruit bright young people and by leaving the task of recruiting staff to the personnel or "human resources" department.

"I hate to mention mcKinsey, Goldman Sachs and Andersen, but if you look at the efforts they devote to recruiting young people at all levels of the organisation, it's not relegated to the human resources department. We don't do that," he said.
Sorrell also said the rising cost of buying television airtime would make TV less and less important to advertisers.
"The importance of TV advertising is going to diminish," he said.
"It is still the most effective medium," he said, but added that its rising cost would drive advertisers increasingly to other media such as radio, print and the Internet.

Sorrell sounded a familiar theme when he told Ogilvy & Mather staff that many ad agencies were clinging to old-fashioned internal management style and failing to be flexible in a fast-changing business environment.
He said the advertising industry considered itself creativite and innovative, but was often complacent and conservative in the way it did business.
"We are as a group dreadfully conservative people," he said.

"We think of ourselves as dreadfully creative and cutting edge. We work with clients who go through major strategic and structural change, yet if we have to go through major strategic and structural change, it takes years," he said.
"We have to learn to be more flexible," sorrell said.
The lack of flexibility helped explain why management consultancies were encroaching on the traditional territory of advertising and marketing services.
Sorrell gave the example of McKinsey, which was hired a few years ago by Unilever Plc to help the Anglo-Dutch conglomerate with branding strategy for its consumer products.
Another example was Safeway Plc, the British supermarket group, which hired McKinsey to advise it on building up the Safeway brand image.
"Why didn't the management of Unilever think that we were capable of doing that?" Sorrell said.
